title: Two Tropical Storms Could Form Back to Back This Week
text:
The eastern Pacific could soon become home to two developing tropical systems tracking across nearly the same stretch of ocean, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC), with forecasters monitoring disturbances south of Baja California that may organize into tropical cyclones over the coming days.
The potential back-to-back development comes as Tropical Storm Lowell continues churning north-northwest of Hawaii. Lowell recently prompted tropical storm warnings in parts of the state and has weakened from its hurricane status earlier this week. Its presence, coupled with the possibility of two new cyclones forming behind it, highlights what has been an active year across the Pacific basin.
Forecasters warned that the Pacific hurricane season could be more active than normal this year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) seasonal outlook called for above-normal activity in the eastern and central Pacific, citing expectations that El Niño conditions would persist through hurricane season. El Niño typically increases tropical cyclone activity across the Pacific by creating a more favorable atmospheric environment for storm formation.
Newsweek reached out to the NHC by email for comment.
Potential Tropical Storms Forecast
One system, designated EP96, has already become increasingly organized several hundred miles south-southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula. The NHC said environmental conditions appear favorable for further development, and a tropical depression is likely to form in the next day or two. Forecasters currently give the disturbance an 80 percent chance of development over 48 hours and a 90 percent chance over the next seven days. The system is moving west-northwest at 10-15 mph.
Meanwhile, a second area of low pressure is forecast to develop several hundred miles south of Baja California this weekend or early next week. While that system does not yet exist, forecasters say gradual development could occur once it forms, with a medium 40 percent chance of becoming a tropical depression within seven days. The disturbance is moving in the same direction as EP96.
The unusual aspect of the forecast is that both systems are expected to emerge in roughly the same general region and follow similar west-northwest tracks away from Mexico and into the open Pacific. If both eventually organize, they could spend part of their lifecycles moving through adjacent stretches of ocean. It's also possible the two systems could get close enough to each other to interact—known as the Fujiwhara effect—that could lead to the storms merging.
For now, EP96 remains the more immediate concern for forecasters. Satellite imagery shows showers and thunderstorms becoming better organized around an elongated area of low pressure, a sign that the system may be consolidating toward a more defined circulation. If organization continues, it could become a tropical depression by late this week.
2026 Atlantic Hurricane Season Forecast
Meanwhile, the Atlantic basin has seen a below-average season after NOAA's outlook issued earlier this year called for a below-normal 2026 Atlantic hurricane season. Forecasters predicted eight to 14 named storms, including three to six hurricanes and one to three major hurricanes of Category 3 strength or higher.
NOAA said the primary reason for the expected reduction in activity is the anticipated development of El Niño, which typically increases wind shear across the Atlantic and makes it more difficult for tropical storms and hurricanes to form and strengthen.
So far this year, there have been five named tropical storms in the Atlantic basin. None reached hurricane status. As of Wednesday morning, there is no tropical storm activity expected in the Atlantic basin over the next seven days.
What Happens Next
In the Pacific Ocean, neither system is forecast to threaten land areas, but their evolution will be watched closely. Once they form, they could cause indirect impacts, such as dangerous waves or rip currents in Baja California.
The eastern Pacific is entering one of its climatologically busiest periods of the year, when ocean temperatures remain warm and atmospheric conditions often favor tropical development.
With Lowell still making headlines near Hawaii and two additional disturbances lining up behind it, the Pacific basin is offering another reminder that the 2026 hurricane season remains far from over. Forecasters will be watching to see whether both areas can capitalize on favorable conditions and become the latest named storms in what has already been a notably active season.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Anna Skinner and Dave Siminoff.

images.caption: A map from the National Hurricane Center shows where two tropical storms could form on top of each other later this week.

title: Hurricane Lowell Live Tracker Maps, Full List of Warnings in Hawaii
text:
Hurricane Lowell remained a powerful storm in the Pacific on Tuesday, but forecasters predicted it would gradually weaken as it continues to move past Hawaii. Even so, officials warned the hurricane could continue generating hazardous surf, heavy rain and gusty winds across parts of the island chain, prompting residents to closely monitor forecasts and advisories.
While Lowell is not expected to strike Hawaii directly, the storm remains large enough to pose risks across the state, particularly along exposed coastlines. Forecasters say dangerous surf, localized flooding and strong winds could still affect portions of the islands as the hurricane passes nearby and begins its anticipated weakening trend.
Hurricane Lowell is expected to weaken to a tropical storm later on Tuesday, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) predicted, and it will remain a tropical storm at least through Sunday.
Hurricane Lowell Live Tracker Maps
As of the most recent NHC update on Tuesday morning, Hurricane Lowell was around 145 miles northwest of Lihue, on Kauai, and moving north, away from Hawaii, at 18 miles per hour. Hurricane Lowell is currently a Category 1 hurricane with maximum sustained wind speeds of 90 mph.
Numerous warnings remain in place as the storm treks further away from Hawaii, with NHC forecasters warning that wind, rain, storm surge, and dangerous surf remain hazardous to Hawaii.
Although Lowell is a Category 1 hurricane, winds are gusting much stronger than its sustained 90 mph. Animated weather footage from windy.com shows some of the strongest gusts clocking in at over 115 mph.
Heavy rain accompanying the storm is also expected to continue, with as much as nearly 3 inches of rain expected over the next 24 hours in Kauai, according to Windy.com.
Waves also remain dangerous, with seas as high as 35 feet near the storm's eye, Windy.com showed. Closer to Hawaii, waves are still large enough to prompt numerous warnings from the local weather office.
Hurricane Lowell: Full List of Hawaii Warnings
Hawaii remained under numerous weather alerts and warnings from the National Weather Service (NWS) on Tuesday. The full list of warnings includes:
- Hurricane Warning: A Hurricane Warning remains in effect for Kauai and Niihau, though forecasters say threats from Lowell are decreasing as the storm moves away and weakens.
- Tropical Storm Warning: A Tropical Storm Warning remains in effect for much of Oahu, including Honolulu, the North Shore, Windward Oahu and the Waianae Coast, where Lowell could bring sustained winds of 15 to 35 mph with gusts as high as 55 mph. Forecasters warned that tropical storm-force winds of 39 to 57 mph remain possible, raising the risk of downed tree limbs, scattered power outages, debris on roadways and hazardous travel conditions.
- High Surf Warning: A High Surf Warning remains in effect through 6 p.m. HST Tuesday for south-facing shores across Hawaii and west-facing shores of the Big Island, where large swells generated by Hurricane Lowell are producing dangerous surf. Wave heights of 20 to 30 feet along parts of Kauai and 15 to 25 feet on some Oahu shores are expected to decline rapidly through the day, but forecasters warned that powerful waves, strong rip currents and ocean water sweeping across beaches, roads and coastal areas could still cause damage to infrastructure and hazardous conditions for motorists and boaters.
- Flood Advisory: A Flood Advisory remains in effect for Oahu until 7:30 a.m. HST as bands of moderate to heavy rain continue moving across the island. Forecasters said rainfall rates of 0.5 to 1 inch per hour could lead to minor flooding on roads, in low-lying and poor-drainage areas, and along streams, with flooding already ongoing or expected to develop. Residents are being urged to avoid streams, drainage ditches and flood-prone areas until conditions improve.
- High Surf Advisory: A High Surf Advisory remains in effect until 6 p.m. HST Tuesday for east-facing shores across Kauai, Oahu, Molokai, Maui and the Big Island, where surf of 7 to 10 feet is creating hazardous ocean conditions. Forecasters warned that strong breaking waves and powerful currents will make swimming dangerous, though surf is expected to gradually subside later in the day.
- Small Craft Advisory: A Small Craft Advisory remains in effect until 6 p.m. HST Tuesday for waters surrounding Maui County and the Big Island, including the Kaiwi, Pailolo and Alenuihaha channels. Forecasters warned that south winds of up to 25 knots and seas reaching 10 feet will create hazardous conditions for small vessels, increasing the risk for inexperienced mariners and those operating smaller boats.
- Flood Watch: A Flood Watch remains in effect through Tuesday afternoon for Kauai, Niihau, Oahu, Maui County and the Big Island as moisture associated with Hurricane Lowell continues to bring periods of heavy rainfall across the state. Forecasters warned that excessive rain could trigger flash flooding, with flood-prone roads, low-lying areas and streams particularly vulnerable to rising water, while rapid runoff could lead to urban flooding and property damage.
What Happens Next
Forecasters expect Hurricane Lowell to continue weakening as it moves away from Hawaii, but its lingering moisture and large swells will keep impacts in place through Tuesday. Flooding rains, gusty winds and hazardous surf are expected to gradually subside later in the day, allowing many warnings and advisories to expire by Tuesday evening if conditions improve as forecast.
Residents are still being urged to monitor updates from the NWS, as localized flooding and dangerous ocean conditions may persist even after the storm pulls farther away.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Sam Wilson.

title: Atlantic Hurricane Season Nears Record as El Niño Keeps Storms at Bay
text:
The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season is approaching a record for the latest formation of its first hurricane, with the basin yet to produce one as it nears its climatological peak.
AccuWeather reported that the latest date for the first Atlantic hurricane of a season during the satellite era was September 11. That happened in both 2002 and 2013. If no hurricane forms by September 11, the 2026 season would pass that benchmark, according to the outlet.
Five named storms have formed so far in the Atlantic as of Tuesday, but none became hurricanes. National Hurricane Center (NHC) data shows that the season so far has produced two fewer named storms, three fewer hurricanes and one fewer major hurricane than the 1991-2020 averages for this point in the year.
AccuWeather attributed the limited activity partly to disruptive wind shear and plumes of dry air associated with Saharan dust. Lead Hurricane Expert Alex DaSilva said the less-favorable environment was expected to persist the rest of the season—through November—and could result in lower overall activity.
"It seems extremely unlikely at this point we will have a hurricane by Friday, which means this season will set the record for the latest [first] hurricane," AccuWeather meteorologist Nick Arman told Newsweek. "If you include all recorded years, counting before satellites going back to the late 1800s, there have been some years that recorded zero hurricanes. However, this has not occurred since 1914 and 1907, well over 100 years ago.
"Another record to watch is the number of hurricane and major hurricanes. There have been a number of years not to record a major hurricane [Category 3 or higher on the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Scale], the most recent being 2013. It is still very uncommon though. However, there have only been two years with zero hurricanes [1907 and 1914], and two years with only one hurricane [1925 and 1905]. None of these are in the satellite era as well."
AccuWeather’s experts are watching an area off the southeastern U.S. where a slow-moving front could increase thunderstorm activity. It assigned the area a low chance of tropical development through the middle of September.
What Is El Niño?
El Niño is the warm phase of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, or ENSO, a recurring Pacific climate pattern that can affect weather worldwide. Its counterpart, La Niña, is the cool phase of the cycle.
Typical El Niño effects can include stormier weather across the southern U.S., drier conditions in some northern areas and changes in hurricane activity.
How El Niño Can Influence Atlantic Hurricanes
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) says El Niño generally reduces Atlantic hurricane activity by increasing vertical wind shear across the basin.
The stronger shear can make it more difficult for thunderstorms to organize and develop into hurricanes, according to NOAA. The agency says El Niño can have the opposite effect in the eastern and central Pacific, where conditions often become more favorable for storm development.
Atlantic Storms That Have Formed in 2026
The NHC’s season summary listed five Atlantic tropical storms as of September 8:
- Arthur: June 17-18.
- Bertha: July 19-23.
- Cristobal: August 12-13.
- Dolly: August 27-28.
- Edouard: August 31-September 2.
2026 Atlantic Storm Names
Below are the official names for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season:
- Arthur
- Bertha
- Cristobal
- Dolly
- Edouard
- Fay
- Gonzalo
- Hanna
- Isaias
- Josephine
- Kyle
- Leah
- Marco
- Nana
- Omar
- Paulette
- Rene
- Sally
- Teddy
- Vicky
- Wilfred
What Happens Next
As of Tuesday, the NHC does not expect tropical cyclone activity in the Atlantic during the next seven days.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and Dave Siminoff.

title: Hurricane Lowell: Most Hawaii Schools Reopen Wednesday, Kauaʻi Stays Closed
text:
As Hurricane Lowell moves away from Hawaii after bringing damaging winds, heavy rain and dangerous surf to parts of the state, most public schools are set to reopen Wednesday, while closures will continue on Kauaʻi and Niʻihau.
Governor Josh Green announced Tuesday that Hawaii Department of Education public schools and offices on Oʻahu, Maui County and Hawaiʻi Island will reopen September 9. All public schools on Kauaʻi will remain closed through Friday because of continuing storm impacts, as will Niʻihau High and Elementary School on the small island of Niʻihau.
“Conditions have improved enough for Oʻahu to fully reopen Wednesday, but Kauaʻi continues to face significant impacts from Hurricane Lowell,” Green said.
“Keeping offices and schools closed in Kauaʻi County will give utility, public works and emergency crews the space they need to safely restore power, clear debris and support affected communities."
State and county offices, University of Hawaiʻi campuses and Judiciary facilities on Oʻahu will also reopen Wednesday as conditions improve following the hurricane.
Officials will reassess conditions throughout the week, with reopening the next week dependent on progress restoring power, clearing roads and debris and ensuring facilities are safe and accessible.
Hurricane Lowell Latest
The center of Lowell passed west of the Hawaiian Islands overnight Tuesday and moved farther away throughout the day. Hurricane warnings for Kauaʻi and Niʻihau were no longer in place by Tuesday morning local time.
Wind gusts reached as high as 80 mph, according to the National Hurricane Center, but sustained winds had weakened by early Tuesday and the storm was expected to continue weakening in the coming days.
In a Tuesday night update, the National Hurricane Center said Lowell was weakening but warned that the threat of flash flooding across the Hawaiian Islands would remain through Wednesday.
As of 11 p.m. ET Tuesday, more than 35,000 customers across Hawaii were without power, according to PowerOutage.us.
Lowell was also generating dangerous surf along the coasts of Mexico’s Baja California and Southern California. Swells producing life-threatening surf and rip currents were expected to continue for the next few days, the hurricane center said.
Residents have been urged to stay off the roads during hazardous conditions, avoid floodwaters and shorelines, prepare for possible power outages, and monitor official forecasts as Lowell moves past the islands.
Green urged people to “remain indoors, avoid unnecessary travel and follow all official emergency instructions.”
Contact Newsweek editor on this story: Edward Pearcey, Gray R. Thomas

This satellite image provided by NOAA shows Hurricane Lowell near Hawaii on Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026. (NOAA via AP)

title: Hurricane Lowell Spaghetti Models Show Possible Path as It Nears Hawaii
text:
Tracker maps show Hurricane Lowell's path across the Pacific as forecasters monitor the powerful storm.
Meteorologists have warned that the system is expected to be almost at major hurricane strength when it moves near the western Hawaiian Islands late Monday, bringing the threat of storm surge and wind impacts for portions of the state.
In an advisory issued Friday, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) said Lowell had weakened slightly to Category 4 strength—the second-highest rating on the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale. An updated advisory Sunday morning said the storm was located around 595 miles south-southwest of Honolulu.
The agency reported maximum sustained winds near 125 miles per hour.
The NHC said fluctuations in strength would be possible this weekend, with a gradual weakening trend expected by early next week. The system was moving west at around 7 mph, with forecasters expecting that motion to continue for the next day or so before a sharp turn to the north or north-northeast on Sunday.
"“Interests in the Hawaiian Islands should monitor the progress of Lowell,” the NHC said. “Watches could be required for portions of the westernmost Hawaiian Islands on Saturday.”"
A hurricane warning was issued Sunday for the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument from Nihoa to French Frigate Shoals while a tropical storm warning was put in effect for Kauai County, including the islands of Kauai and Niihau, the NWS said in an updated advisory.
Rainfall and Surf Threats
The NHC is also warning of heavy rainfall and dangerous coastal conditions across Hawaii as Lowell approaches. According to the agency, Kauai and the Big Island could receive three to six inches of rain, with isolated totals exceeding 10 inches possible.
Maui is forecast to receive two to four inches, with isolated amounts up to eight inches possible, while other islands could see one to two inches of rainfall, with localized totals reaching four inches.
"Lowell expected to produce heavy rains and possible flash flooding across the entire state of Hawaii over the next couple of days," the advisory from the NHC said Sunday.
The NHC said the rainfall may lead to flash flooding and mudslides, particularly in areas of steep terrain.
The agency also warned that swells generated by Lowell are expected to affect many of the Hawaiian Islands over the next several days, creating life-threatening surf and rip current conditions.
Three Hurricanes Churn in Pacific
Lowell is not the only hurricane being monitored in the Pacific. In earlier advisories, the NHC said Hurricane Karina was located about 825 miles east of Hilo, Hawaii, with maximum sustained winds of 75 mph.
Karina was moving northwest at around 8 mph and is forecast to turn west-northwest over the next day or two. The NHC said additional weakening is likely in the coming days and that Karina is expected to become post-tropical by Monday.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Marie was located about 635 miles west of the southern tip of Baja California with maximum sustained winds of about 90 mph.
The storm was moving northwest near 8 mph, a motion the NHC expects to continue for the next several days. Forecasters said a gradual weakening trend is expected to continue.
Contact Newsweek editor on this story: Edward Pearcey.

title: Hawaii Issues Warning as Category 5 Hurricane Lowell Nears: Live Tracker Maps
text:
A tropical storm warning has been issued for Hawaii's offshore waters as powerful Hurricane Lowell churns through the Central Pacific, prompting forecasters to warn of strengthening winds, building seas and dangerous marine conditions around the islands through the end of the week.
As of the most recent update from the National Hurricane Center (NHC) on Wednesday, Hurricane Lowell had maximum sustained winds of 160 mph, making it a major Category 5 hurricane. Lowell is likely to remain a powerful hurricane through the end of the week, the NHC said.
The storm is generating large swells and hazardous conditions that have triggered a series of marine and wind advisories across the state. On Tuesday night, the National Weather Service (NWS) office in Honolulu issued a tropical storm warning for Hawaii's offshore waters, warning of "significant" seas up to 18 feet.
"Swells generated by Lowell are likely to affect portions of the Hawaiian Islands beginning on Wednesday," the NHC said. "These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions."
Animated weather footage from windy.com illustrated the extent of the large waves.
As of the most recent NHC update, Lowell was around 445 miles south of Hilo, Hawaii. The storm was moving west at 10 mph.
Will Hurricane Lowell Make Landfall in Hawaii?
No. Current forecasts from the NHC show Lowell's eye passing south of Hawaii as a major hurricane. It will continue churning out to sea through at least Sunday night and is expected to retain its major hurricane status through then.
Lowell arrives after a notably active hurricane season for Hawaii, underscoring that the eye of a tropical cyclone does not need to make landfall to create dangerous conditions across the islands. Earlier storms this year brought impacts ranging from heavy rainfall and flooding concerns to damaging surf and hazardous marine conditions, even when their centers remained offshore.
Forecasters are emphasizing a similar message with Lowell: While the hurricane's forecast track keeps it away from a direct strike on Hawaii, its large wind field and powerful swells are already prompting warnings for offshore waters and advisories across multiple islands.
Hurricane Lowell's Projected Path Toward Hawaii—Tracker
Animated weather footage from windy.com shows the storm trekking south of Hawaii on Wednesday. Although the eye of the storm won't make landfall on any of the Hawaiian Islands, meteorologists at the NWS office in Honolulu have issued several wind advisories.
Eastern winds between 25 and 35 mph with some gusts reaching up to 55 mph are expected across parts of Kahoolawe, Lanai, Maui, Molokai and the Big Island between noon local time Wednesday and 6 a.m. Friday.
"Winds will be strongest through passes and higher terrain of the North and South Kohala Districts, and near South Point on the Big Island, through the central valley on Maui, and the higher elevations of Maui County," the advisory said. "Winds this strong can tear off shingles, knock down tree branches, blow away tents and awnings and make it difficult to steer, especially for drivers of high profile vehicles."
The advisory urged people to remain alert for falling tree branches and to prepare for power outages.
When Does Hawaii's Hurricane Season End?
Hawaii's hurricane season runs from June 1 through November 30, aligning with the Central Pacific hurricane season monitored by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Central Pacific Hurricane Center. While tropical cyclones can occasionally form outside those dates, the vast majority develop during this six-month period when ocean temperatures and atmospheric conditions are most favorable. Hurricane activity in the Central Pacific typically peaks between July and October, with September often among the busiest months.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Anna Skinner, Dave Siminoff, Anna Commander, Gray R. Thomas

title: Tropical Storm Edouard Spaghetti Models Show Impact Zone Through Texas
text:
Tropical Storm Edouard is bringing heavy rain, flooding concerns, and travel disruptions across parts of Texas, as the system moves inland from the Gulf Coast.
While the storm has weakened to a tropical depression, forecasters warn that the most significant threat remains widespread rainfall capable of triggering dangerous flash flooding across several regions of the state.
The latest spaghetti models show Edouard tracking northward through eastern and central Texas, with the heaviest rainfall corridor extending inland from the upper Texas coast.
Although uncertainty remains over the precise path of the storm's remnants, the models collectively point to a broad impact zone stretching from the Gulf Coast into eastern and central Texas, matching forecasts that call for the heaviest rainfall and greatest flood risk in those areas.
Edouard's Shift From Wind to Rain Threat
According to the National Hurricane Center (NHC), tropical storm force wind gusts—classified as sustained winds of between 39 and 73 mph, according to the National Weather Service (NWS)—remain possible near the center of the storm for several hours, but heavy rainfall has become the primary hazard.
The agency is warning that river and flash flooding (particularly in urban areas) is likely from the upper Texas coast through east-central Texas and into far southwest Louisiana as the storm continues inland.
Texas Communities Brace for Flooding
Local officials across southeast Texas have been preparing for the storm's impacts.
According to local news reports, in Montgomery County, emergency managers mobilized equipment, coordinated with state partners and secured additional resources, including rescue boats, as flooding concerns grew. Schools including Conroe ISD and Willis ISD canceled classes on Wednesday, while some government offices also shut down ahead of the storm.
Jason Millsaps, executive director of the Montgomery County Office of Homeland Security and Emergency Management, said the biggest concern is heavy rain bands that can remain over one area for an extended period, dumping significant amounts of rain in a short time.
Officials have also positioned barricades at flood-prone locations throughout the county.
Flood Watches Span Large Parts of Texas
The NWS has also issued Flood Watches covering multiple regions of northeast, east-central and southeast Texas.
In Henderson County and the east-central Texas counties of Anderson, Freestone and Leon, forecasters say most locations can expect between 1 and 3 inches of rainfall through Wednesday until Thursday night, although isolated totals of 4 to 6 inches are possible. Excessive runoff could lead to flooding of rivers, creeks, streams and other low-lying areas.
Further south and east, a broader Flood Watch covers Brazos, Chambers, Harris, Liberty, Montgomery, Polk, San Jacinto, Trinity, Walker and several neighboring counties.
Forecasters expect more significant impacts in this region. Rainfall totals of 3 to 6 inches are forecast, with isolated locations potentially receiving between 10 and 15 inches, particularly along and east of Interstate 45. Rainfall rates may exceed 3 to 4 inches per hour during the most intense downpours.
What Happens Next?
Forecasters expect Edouard's remnants to continue moving inland through Wednesday and Thursday, spreading periods of moderate to heavy rain across eastern Texas.
Even as the storm weakens, flood risks are expected to persist because saturated areas could receive repeated rounds of rainfall.
Emergency officials are urging residents to closely monitor forecasts and heed flood warnings if conditions worsen.
Authorities are also emphasizing a familiar message: drivers should never attempt to cross flooded roadways because water depths can be difficult to judge and conditions can change rapidly.
Newsweek contacted Governor Greg Abbott's office for comment. The office responded by sharing an official August 31 press release addressing the state's preparations for the tropical weather threat.
Key Takeaway
For many Texans, the biggest danger from Edouard is no longer wind.
Instead, forecasters warn that the storm could leave behind a trail of flooding rainfall capable of inundating roads, neighborhoods, and waterways well after the tropical system itself has weakened.
Contact Newsweek editor on this story: Edward Pearcey.

title: Hurricane Karina Live Tracker Map Shows Trajectory of Storm
text:
Hurricane Karina continues to churn across the eastern Pacific on Tuesday as a powerful Category 4 storm, with forecasters tracking its west-northwestward path over open ocean.
The latest Hurricane Karina update shows the storm moving west-northwest at about 10 miles per hour, well away from Mexico and other populated areas. Forecasts indicate Karina will remain over open waters while gradually weakening later this week, though it is expected to maintain hurricane strength for several days as it continues deeper into the Pacific. Forecasters have not issued any coastal watches or warnings, and the storm is not currently forecast to make landfall.
While Karina poses no immediate threat to land, the storm has generated large swells that can produce dangerous surf and rip currents. Earlier advisories warned that those swells could affect portions of southwestern Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula, creating hazardous beach conditions even hundreds of miles from the hurricane's center.
When Did Hurricane Karina Form?
Karina strengthened into a hurricane on Sunday after forming as a tropical storm last Thursday.
Animated satellite imagery from windy.com shows Hurricane Karina about 1,210 miles west-southwest of the southwestern tip of Baja California. Other tropical storms, including Tropical Storm Lowell to the left and Tropical Storm Marie to the right, are also visible in the live animated footage.
What Areas Could Be Impacted by Hurricane Karina?
Hurricane Karina is not expected to make direct landfall; it is currently churning in the central Pacific Ocean. However, strong swells and rip currents can be felt hundreds of miles away from the storm, and the NHC warned of a moderate risk of rip currents in Southern California.
"Swells generated by Karina will affect portions of the coast of southwest Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula for the next couple of days and will likely spread northward to southern California through midweek," the public advisory said. "These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions."
Animated tracker maps from windy.com show strong waves around the storm but calmer waters closer to land.
What Spaghetti Models Show
Spaghetti models, which combine forecasts from multiple weather prediction models into a single graphic, show Hurricane Karina continuing on a generally west-northwest track across the open eastern Pacific with relatively little disagreement among forecasters.
The models also indicate that Karina is near its peak intensity and should steadily weaken later this week as environmental conditions become less favorable. As of Tuesday morning, Karina was a powerful Category 4 hurricane with sustained winds of 140 mph.
Where Is Tropical Storm Edouard?
As of Tuesday morning, Tropical Storm Edouard was located in the northwestern Gulf of Mexico just off the Texas-Louisiana coast. The NHC placed the storm's center about 30 miles south of Cameron, Louisiana, and 50 miles southeast of Port Arthur, Texas. Edouard was moving northwest at about 8 mph with sustained winds of 50 mph, and forecasters said it was expected to continue strengthening before reaching the northwestern Gulf Coast later Tuesday.
Will Tropical Storm Edouard Hit Texas?
Yes. The forecast track calls for the center to make landfall near the Texas-Louisiana border before moving inland across southeast Texas, bringing the threat of heavy rain, flooding, storm surge and gusty winds.
When Does Hurricane Season 2026 End?
Hurricane season officially ends on November 30, though forecasters note that tropical systems can occasionally develop outside that window. Historically, in the Atlantic basin, storm activity peaks in early September.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Kate Nalepinski and Sam Wilson.

title: Live Tracker Maps as Tropical Rainstorm Set to Hit US Coast
text:
A tropical rainstorm churning across the northern Gulf Coast is expected to bring rounds of heavy rain, localized flash flooding and travel disruptions to parts of Texas and Louisiana this week, with forecasters warning that some communities could receive several inches of rainfall in a short period of time.
While the system is not expected to become a major wind event, forecasters say rain will be the primary hazard as it approaches the coast.
The National Hurricane Center (NHC) on Monday began issuing advisories on Potential Tropical Cyclone Five, a disturbance in the northwestern Gulf that was producing sustained winds of 35 miles per hour. Tropical storm warnings were issued for portions of the upper Texas and southwestern Louisiana coastline as the system moved west-northwestward at about 5 mph.
Forecasters say the disturbance has a window to strengthen before coming ashore. AccuWeather reported the rainstorm could briefly organize enough to become either a tropical depression or a tropical storm before making landfall Tuesday, although significant intensification is not expected. If it reaches tropical-storm strength, the next name on the Atlantic list would be Edouard.
The heaviest rainfall is forecast to first affect coastal Louisiana before spreading westward into southeastern Texas, including the Houston metropolitan area.
Rainfall Forecast as Map Reveals Impacts
Animated weather footage from windy.com shows heavy rain over the next few days across coastal Texas and Louisiana. Some areas will see as much 9 inches of rain.
"PTC Five is expected to produce rainfall totals of 3 to 6 inches with maximum totals of 9 inches for parts of the Upper Texas Coast inland through east-central Texas, with 2 to 3 inches for Southwest Louisiana," the NHC said. "This rainfall could produce flash flooding, especially in low-lying and urban areas."
According to AccuWeather, widespread rainfall totals of 1 to 2 inches are expected along the Louisiana coast and into eastern Texas through midweek, with a corridor of 2 to 4 inches possible around Houston and southeastern Texas. Some locations could see considerably higher totals where thunderstorms repeatedly move over the same areas. AccuWeather's Local StormMax forecast indicates that isolated locations could receive as much as 12 inches of rain through Wednesday.
Forecasters expect showers and thunderstorms to increase across Louisiana on Monday before spreading into coastal Texas Monday night and Tuesday. Houston and surrounding communities are expected to experience the most persistent rainfall from late Monday into Tuesday, raising the risk of flooded roadways and travel delays during peak commuting hours.
Satellite imagery available through windy.com shows the storm approaching the coast late Monday morning.
Even in places that do not receive the highest rainfall totals, intense downpours could quickly overwhelm drainage systems and produce standing water in low-lying areas. Officials often warn motorists not to drive through flooded streets, as water depth can be difficult to judge and road surfaces may be damaged beneath the floodwaters.
Wind impacts are expected to be secondary. Forecasters say the system could bring locally gusty winds near the coast and within stronger thunderstorms, along with rough surf and hazardous conditions for small craft in the northern Gulf. However, widespread damaging winds or significant coastal inundation are not currently anticipated.
After moving inland over southeastern Texas, the system is expected to weaken rapidly and lose organization. Tropical moisture is forecast to linger across the Gulf Coast through much of the week, allowing additional showers and thunderstorms to develop from Texas eastward across the central Gulf Coast and into Florida. That means localized flooding concerns may persist even after the system itself dissipates.
Contact Newsweek editor for this story: Anthony Murray.

title: Hurricane Karina Spaghetti Models As California Faces Life-Threatening Waves
text:
Hurricane Karina has strengthened into a powerful Category 4 storm over the eastern Pacific, and swells generated by the storm are expected to spread north toward Southern California, bringing potentially life-threatening surf and rip-current conditions.
An advisory from NOAA's National Hurricane Center (NHC) states: "Swells generated by Karina will affect portions of the coast of southwest Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula for the next couple of days and will likely spread northward to southern California on Monday through midweek. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions."
Hurricane Karina itself is not forecast to track toward California. The storm is moving westward, farther out into the Pacific.
The California threat comes from the swells generated by the hurricane, which can travel hundreds of miles ahead of and away from the storm.
Karina was about 1,020 miles (1,640 kilometers) west-southwest of the southern tip of Baja California late Sunday, according to the NHC. The hurricane had maximum sustained winds of 145 mph and was moving west at 9 mph. There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.
Newsweek contacted NOAA via email on Monday for comment.
Hurricane Karina Spaghetti Models
The latest spaghetti-model guidance on Tropical Tidbits, a meteorological website and data visualization platform specializing in tropical cyclone tracking, weather analysis, and forecasting, shows Karina continuing generally westward over the open Pacific, with forecast tracks keeping the center of the hurricane well offshore of Mexico and California.
The maps use various acronyms. GEFS stands for Global Ensemble Forecast System, a weather model that runs many slightly different forecasts to show a range of possible storm tracks. Tracks is the predicted paths of the storm's center from those different forecasts. MSLP means minimum mean sea level pressure. This is the lowest atmospheric pressure the storm is expected to reach. Mb denotes millibars, the unit used to measure atmospheric pressure, whereas hPa means hectopascals, the standard unit meteorologists use for atmospheric pressure. A lower MSLP generally means a stronger storm.
Life-Threatening Surf Could Reach Southern California
The NHC's latest forecast has Karina continuing west Monday before turning west-northwest Tuesday. The hurricane is expected to remain over the Pacific.
The agency said swells generated by Karina would affect parts of southwest Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula over the next couple of days before likely spreading northward to Southern California from Monday through midweek.
Those swells are expected to create life-threatening surf and rip-current conditions, as per the NHC's warning.
Karina Forecast To Remain Offshore
Karina's center was located near 17.2 degrees north latitude and 124.4 degrees west longitude at 0900 UTC Monday. The storm was moving west at about 8 knots, with maximum sustained winds of 125 knots and gusts reaching 150 knots, according to the NHC's forecast advisory.
The NHC said additional strengthening was possible Monday, followed by fluctuations in intensity through the middle of the week.
The latest forecast track takes Karina still further into the Pacific.
Beachgoers Urged To Check Local Conditions
People planning to visit Southern California beaches should check the latest forecasts and warnings from their local weather office as the swells arrive.
The NHC specifically urged the public to consult local weather-office products regarding the surf and rip-current threat.
